Gabriel Knight: Sins of the Father é o primeiro adventure da Sierra que eu joguei, tendo sido fã dos jogos da Lucasarts minha vida toda, e posso afirmar que com certeza vou me aprofundar mais em jogos da empresa e principalmente dessa série e de sua criadora, Jane Jansen, depois de jogá-lo. Gostei muito da história e do universo criado, e bastante também com a extensa pesquisa que claramente foi feita acerca dos elementos históricos e religiosos presentes aqui, sendo bem mais respeitoso do que eu esperava de um jogo de 1993 - enquanto o jogo é sobre a investigação dos "Assassinatos Vodu", houve um esforço enorme para explicar diversos dos elementos dessa cultura e fazer uma distinção entre "voodoo" e "black voodoo". O jogo também se passa em Nova Orleans e apresenta vários locais de verdade da cidade.

Os visuais, por mais que tenham uma resolução pequena, são bem bonitos, principalmente pra época, além de apresentarem alguns visuais desconcertantes que eu não estava esperando. Várias das cutscenes também foram claramente inspiradas por quadrinhos e graphic novels, com divisões em painéis (exemplificado mais ainda pela graphic novel que vinha junto do jogo fisicamente na época). O jogo é voltado para o público adulto, e por conta disso apresenta momentos de violência e gore. As músicas aqui variam entre boas e excelentes, o tema principal é com certeza um destaque. As vozes no geral também são bem boas, com grande parte sendo composta de atores de Hollywood, como o Tim Curry como Gabriel Knight e o Mark Hamill como Detetive Mosely.

Quanto à falhas, tive algumas que incomodaram um pouco em minha experiência. Do áudio, o maior problema é a voz da narradora, que eu achei bem ruim e destoa do tom do resto do jogo. De escrita, tiveram algumas piadas e quebras da quarta parede que achei que destoaram um pouco demais também, e achei uma ou duas observações que entregam surpresas do enredo antes da hora. Nos sistemas do jogo, eu tive problemas principalmente numa parte envolvendo tambores, a interface não é nada intuitiva e eu só descobri que tinha mais páginas que eu precisava usar lendo o manual do jogo. E eu teria incluído a graphic novel que vinha com o jogo junto do manual em um PDF, tive que pesquisar na internet pra ler.

Mas o maior problema que a maioria vai achar quando jogar se trata da emulação: o jogo presente aqui na Steam roda pelo DOSbox, e no geral a emulação funciona muito bem, mas existem certos momentos envolvendo timing que a velocidade do emulador não permite que o jogador faça as ações necessárias dentro do tempo. Isso pode ser resolvido entrando na pasta do jogo e editando o valor do "cycles" dentro do arquivo "dosboxGK.conf" para uns 10000, fazendo a ação e depois editando de novo para "max", mas é um processo que é chato e devia ter sido minimamente testado antes de ser lançado aqui na Steam - mas infelizmente, para quem gosta de jogar esses jogos antigos de PC, faz parte.

Eu com certeza recomendo Gabriel Knight: Sins of the Father para quem gosta de jogos adventure, e mal posso esperar para jogar o resto dos jogos da série.

Es difícil definir con palabras un juego de aventuras gráficas (hoy llamadas de point and click) que me acompañó por buena parte de la vida: habré tenido 12 o 13 años cuando en la vieja PC conseguí jugar a Gabriel Knight. En esa oportunidad me ocurrió algo: no había internet y apenas existían algunas revistas especializadas de juego de PC y la que tenía (Pcjuegos si no le erro) no tenía una solución correcta a un mensaje que hay que dejar en una lápida (DJ Sekey…para no espolear, no la pondré de forma completa). Hoy, pasados más de quince años, aún recuerdo esa frase y la frustración de no poder terminar el juego. Terminé alquilando el CD (si, en ese momento se podían alquilar juegos los fin de semanas en Argentina) y lo pasé en inglés. Fue tal la necesidad de terminar esa historia, que apenas consiguiendo acompañar los diálogos, la historia me entraba por los ojos.
Pero esa no fue la única vez que jugué Gabriel Knight. Jugué su reedición y lo habré jugados una o dos veces más, en su versión original. Ahora apenas lo instalé, pero se me pone la piel de gallina al escuchar la música cuando aparece el menú principal, previo el logo de sierra. 
Diría que es entre las mejores aventuras gráficas que jugué en mi vida. En mi adolescencia era mi género favorito y hoy cada tanto juego alguna que otra. Pero me gustaría nombrar algunos puntos que hacen de este título un imprescindible, mismo pasado tantos años: a) La historia: la imaginación de la escritora Jane Jensen deslumbra. Si te gustan las historias de brujas en Nueva Orleans, la existencia de una secta y cazadores de demonios, no lo dudes, esta es tu historia. Es fascinante lo bien hilada y contada que está la historia. Realmente es una historia de investigación, densa, de muchos diálogos, entender pistas, de interpretarlas. No son tan complejas como las de las secuelas siguientes (sobre todo la tercera parte), pero requiere de usar un poco la materia gris para resolver acertijos. B) Aunque quizás quedó viejo un poco la vieja usanza del menú de acciones a realizar, sin dudas, para quienes nos formamos en aquellos años, no hay mejor comodidad que ella. Es un juego de Sierra, con lo cual, menú de acciones y objetos hacen parte, pero también la posibilidad de aplicar objetos sobre otros, para obtener bosquejos, frases en un cuaderno, que se torna esencial para realizar acciones (como usar el teléfono, recuperar pistas, etc.) C) La música: sin dudas las melodías, para ser de aquella época, están muy bien logradas, acompañan el misterio y la tensión y hay algunas de ellas que son imborrables de la memoria. D) la jugabilidad: mismo siendo una aventura gráfica, ya aparece aquí la posibilidad de que nuestro personaje perezca mediante ciertas acciones o situaciones, lo que también agrega una cuota de atención del jugador a lo que está haciendo. 

Realmente es una pena que no tengamos más Gabriel Knight. Lo último que supe es de un desentendimiento entre la productora del juego y su creadora, la autora Jensen. Mismo así, para quienes gustamos de aventuras gráficas complejas, con grandes historias, ya esta primera entrega cumple con creces. ¡Vivan los Schattenjäger!

'Gabriel Knight: Sins of the Father' is the first in an increasingly-lackluster series of horror-themed dramatic adventure games.

New Orleans is threatened by a series of mysterious Voodoo murders, and our hero soon finds himself deep in the investigation -- which spans from the swamplands and Plantation houses of the deep south, to snowswept cliffside castles in the German countryside.  Gabriel will discover secrets about the case -- and his own family lineage -- which will change his world, forever.

A point & click narrative adventure with a full voice cast and realistic art design & direction.
The puzzles and goals are often more frustrating than they are fun, and the control options are overabundant and in desperate need of streamlining.
The voicework, which was only available on the CD-ROM edition back in the big box days, is the highlight -- with Tim Curry as our protagonist, making a terrible attempt at a southern drawl, and the bubbly Lea Remini playing his sassy Asian secretary.  Mark Hamill makes a few appearances, as well as other notable cameos.

If you're a fan of the genre, you could do a lot worse...like any of the sequels.

I have mixed feelings about this game and would not advise to attempt playing this without at least a basic hint guide system. Some of the puzzles require specific answers which may not be straight forward such as where the player needs to write out a coded message letter by letter and match the exact phrasing the game is looking for. At other times, using items in the game world almost feels random leaving the player frantically trying ANYTHING to get the story to progress. I ran into several bugs due to compatibility issues which required workarounds. Still, MOST of the puzzles and adventures in this game were satisfying and enjoyable with a few truly giving you that "AHA!" moment. 

The dialogue and conversations are fairly well handled with Gabriel investigating each person he meets. This could have been structured better however. Perhaps the most frustrating thing is how conversations branch, or more so that they don't requiring the player to ask the same question sometimes half a dozen times to receive the answer they need. This means the dialogue sometimes feels unnatural and canned but it is interesting to see how each person you meet responds to different topics. 

I found the voice acting to range from great to awkward. Ultimately, Tim Curry is a marvelous actor and amazing character but having an Englishman attempt a Cajun accent is ill advised at best. He just barely pulls it off for no lack of trying on his part. It simply isn't a good role for him. He also voices a butler in the game which was a nice little nod to his previous work. The other casting is spot on and immersive with good acting throughout. 

Most of the writing is great with some speedbumps. Gabriel's relationship with Malia feels half baked and ill conceived. One minute she barely tolerates him, the next she is throwing herself at him. His relationship with his assistant Grace is outright inappropriate. Still, he manages to be a lovable character and the mythology they weave is interesting. Where this game shines is the art and writing which make it worthwhile. The story gets truly interesting when Gabriel reconnects with his ancestry and learns of a deeper plot dating back hundreds of years. I would honestly love to have seen a Gabriel Knight television show full of mysteries. Ultimately I felt that the ending wasn't very satisfying and felt abrupt so I would like to know how things turned out for him after the adventure. 

I enjoyed the game and want to check out the sequel. If you like games like King's Quest or Monkey Island I'm sure you will like this too.

I never played this game when it came out, but I recently replayed Beneath a Steel Sky and was looking for something kind of similar and I saw this game on a lot of lists of point and clicks.  So I am going into this review without any nostalgia or "I remember whens".  This game is good.  It is very good.  It's not great but it definitely makes you want to see what happens next.  

The Good:  

The story is phenomenal.  I learned so much useless information about Louisianan Voodoo and African tribal mythology that I couldn't help but be interested in.  The voice acting is also amazing.  As stated in other reviews, a whole host of famous stars lend their voices to the characters of this game.

The Bad:

One of the biggest gripes is the graphics.  I realize this is almost 30 years old but the graphics make it really hard to see important items that you need to pick up or objects that you need to interact with.  There were times where I was stuck, looked up a walkthrough, and found out there is something I need to pick up right in front of me but all I can see is blurry pixels.  Again, its an old game but it is a lot harder to make out items than other games from the time period.  One other gripe I have is that I feel they purposely made a few puzzles intentionally obscure and difficult to drum up business for the Sierra help line.  One example of this is writing the message on the wall.  No idea how we are supposed to come up with that message.

The Verdict:  As I said, this is a good game.  I don't think it is the best point and click, I think Indiana Jones and the Fate of Atlantis still holds that spot but for the price there is more than enough here to keep you entertained.  Also it is a nice length.  The entire game can be beaten in under 10 hours even if you are taking your time or get stuck a few times.  I recommend checking it out.
I did need to reference the Gabriel Knight Sierra hintbook a few times to get it through it. It was so much fun.

Gabriel Knight: Sins of the Father is a classic Point & Click Adventure game from Sierra and has two more games in the series.  Though I was certainly playing Sierra games when this first came out... I had never played this game.  I had always heard how fantastic it was but just never got around to it.  So I finally purchased it on STEAM and gave it a go.

The story and characters are absolutely fantastic in this game.  The story isn't overly predictable and has several twists.  The characters are well developed and have a lot of interesting backstory and personality.  There really isn't anything I would complain about in terms of the story.  This game is not a short game and offers a lot of dialogue and reading material.  The dialogues while they do actually end up being pretty extensive are generally revealed in relatively short snippets for you to discover over the course of the first 6 (of the overall 10) in-game days.  There are some dialogue options that are optional and serve only to flesh out the story and character more but, I really liked and appreciated that they were there for just that reason.

The game is almost 30 years old (at the time of writing this review) so yeah, the graphics when compared to modern graphics aren't fantastic.  If you played this back in the 90's you probably won't care and if your a newer gamer who for some reason just can't deal with pixelated retro type graphics in a game then I guess your not going to like this  game but the good news is you can experience most of this games fantastic qualities with updated graphics by checking out the newer anniverary edition of this game which has updated graphics.  Why, would anyone choose this older version over the new one besides nostalgia you might ask?  For me it came down to one reason... TIM CURRY!  The new one has a completely new voice cast and I just love Tim Curry's voice.

This game actually had an amazing voice cast.  Not only did it have Tim Curry voicing the titular character Gabriel Knight it also has Mark Hamil (Luke Skywalker) voicing his best friend and Michael Dorn (Worf from Star Trek: TNG) voicing Dr. John.  His friend Grace is voiced by Leah Remini (Carrie from King of Queens) and the desk sergeant is voice by Jim Cummings (the voice of Tigger).  There are actually quite a few notable names in this voice cast!  The characters are all very professionally voiced and well recorded and the actors all did a fantastic job with voicing their characters expressing emotions and getting the right tones for the conversations.  There aren't really any awkward conversations, it was well written and well voiced. 

The gameplay is good, there's a nice mix and ratio of exploration, dialogue, and puzzle.  The puzzles themselves aren't terribly hard but, you my find you need a little help from UHS or a walkthrough on some of the puzzles.  Like the "Sekey Madoule" for example... how I was supposed to arrive at that naturally as the solution and then figure out that's what I should write, let alone remember the spelling?  I don't know.  For those who've played the game, you probably know what I'm talking about, for those who haven't, I hope this doesn't give too much away.  Other than that, I didn't need hints very often but I did need them a few times.  If you end up finding yourself stuck don't forget to revisit dialogues you've already had.  Sometimes new responses (or additional ones) are available.

The UI is probably the only thing I didn't like.  Though I'm familiar with the style of UI there were some superfluous aspects that actually made game play more annoying.  While most P&C clicks especially from Sierra had the Walk, Look, Talk, Touch icons along with the most recent/ative inventory item that could rotate through on right-click this game had 4 icons that would nomally all be handled by the touch/hand one (pick up, open/close, operate, push/pull) and two for talk (interrogate and talk?) along with the walk and look icons for a total of 9 icons to rotate through as opposed to the usual 5 and it made right clicking through them slower than just selecting them from the action bar at the top.

The second issue I had with the UI is that in dialogues the topics don't show up as grayed out or a different color when you have already used that topic and that makes it difficult to tell if there are other responses often you need to click the same topic multiple times to get all the information.

At the beginning of the game I thought this was actually a bit impressive in terms of diversity and representation.  It had a strong, rich, smart, beautiful black woman as a major character... the protagonist (though a white man) also has a close friend/employee who's an Asian woman.  Many of the characters are actually black, etc... but then as I continued on in the game it became more noticeable how many stereotypes are still present and how the cultural appropriation so common of the 90's globalization ideals were actually present in the game.  For example, there's a fortune teller dressed in bellydance clothes who performs belly dance in the park... even though she's not in any way representing Arab's or Arab culture.  The Hippie-like Vouduine (sp?) Magentia Moonbeam also performs belly dance with her snake.  Bellydance has nothing to do with Voodoo or Hippies or anything and she seems very much like just a white woman who has appropriated the heck out of several cultures and practices. 

I did feel they actually represented a fair amount of accuracy when talking about Voodoo though.  Sure there were still some stereotypes (some were addressed in game as stereotypes even) but, there was also a lot of information that was true even if it mostly lead more into fantasy and fiction than true history and fact.  It did however go to great lengths to present some of that only to have the characters actually promoting and being those same stereotypes they were denying.

Though, I ended up leaving the launcher running on my computer for some time which continues to count as the game running, I believe my actual game play time for me at the time of writing this was closer to 12-15 hours.    That makes this game about $0.40-$0.50/hr of gameplay.  So even at full price this game would be worth the cost in my opinion but it does go on sale frequently enough that you could get an even better deal.

I don't know how I missed this in the 90s during my golden adventure gaming period. This was a great game that was a lot of fun, didn't contain any overly challenging puzzles, and genuinely made me want to finally go and visit the French Quarter.

Charming graphics with well done pixels, fantastic voice acting, and an easy interface makes this a breeze. There are, of course, frustrating adventure game tropes of the era, like pixel hunting for that one thing (I missed the key sketchbook item which REALLY set me back on Day 1 - not a good look), or trying to follow game logic rather than... logic. For example, in a key part of the game I showed two inventory items to a character and it did not progress the plot. I traveled around for ages and could not figure out what to do, unitl I broke down and hit a guide; I had to COMBINE the two items in my inventory and THEN show them to the character. -_-

But overall this is really a must have if you're down for that retro style and solid gameplay. But with any game like this KEEP A PEN AND PAPER handy and write stuff down! That's how you did it back in the day - and how I solved the "notorious" clock puzzle without any difficulty. :)
